pos: n. (the region of the Italian heel, holding Greek-rite villages and Waldensian colonies until the suppression of 1561)
etymology: From Latin Apulia, the land of the Apuli, an Italic people of the south-east.
biblical_def: Apulia is the long region of the Italian heel, a country of olive plains, limestone and harbours facing Greece. Two things set it apart in church history. It kept Greek-rite Christian villages for centuries after the rest of the peninsula was Latin, a legacy of Byzantine rule, with Greek liturgy and married clergy surviving in pockets into the modern period; the Latinisation of those parishes was pressed from the sixteenth century onward. And it held colonies of Waldenses who had migrated from the Alpine valleys in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries into Apulia and Calabria, farming settlements that kept their own barbes, their own books and a quiet separation from the parish. In 1559 and 1560 those colonies were discovered to have openly joined the Reformed churches; in 1561 the viceroy of Naples and the Inquisition destroyed them, with massacres, galley sentences and forced dispersal. The dictionary records Apulia for both: a region that preserved an older Christianity that Rome eventually suppressed, and that sheltered a confessing people whose end was violent and almost entirely forgotten.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country; a rite as the form of a religious ceremony; dispersion as the act of scattering; a remnant as that which is left; and suppression as the act of putting down.
webster_full: COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it.
RITE, n. The manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept or custom; a formal act of religion.
DISPERSION, n. The act of scattering; the state of being scattered or separated into remote parts.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of suppressing, crushing or putting an end to; the act of concealing or keeping back.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
corruption_summary: Region of the Italian heel which kept Greek-rite villages and Waldensian farming colonies until the suppression of 1561 under the viceroy of Naples.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the quiet erasure of a confessing people, which is a different crime from the famous massacres and is easier to commit. The Apulian and Calabrian Waldenses had lived for a century or more as farmers who paid their rents and kept their own teachers, and when they identified themselves publicly with the Reformed churches they were destroyed in a single season and left almost no record. John sees such people and gives their deaths a location that no archive can take away: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the doctrine of the remnant. Scripture insists repeatedly that God keeps a small number when the visible body has gone over, and it treats that number as his doing rather than theirs: “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). Isaiah says what would have happened without it, “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9), and Hebrews gives the verdict on the hunted that the world never gives them: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38). A colony of farmers in the heel of Italy is exactly the sort of thing the dictionary exists to keep from being lost twice.

pos: n. (the region of the Italian toe, home of Joachim of Fiore and of the Waldensian colony at Guardia Piemontese destroyed in 1561)
etymology: From Latin Calabria, originally the name of the Apulian peninsula, transferred to the toe in the Byzantine period.
biblical_def: Calabria is the mountainous toe of Italy, Greek in rite and often in speech until the later Middle Ages. Two names attach to it. Joachim of Fiore, abbot of San Giovanni in Fiore and died about 1202, divided history into three ages of Father, Son and Spirit and announced a coming age of the Spirit in which the institutional church would be superseded; his scheme was condemned in part, but it fed radical Franciscan expectation for three centuries and is the ancestor of every Christian progressivism that treats a new era as the key to Scripture. And Guardia Piemontese, a village founded by Waldensian settlers from the Alps, was destroyed in 1561 after the colony declared for the Reformed faith: the inhabitants were besieged, taken, and killed or sent to the galleys, and the gate of the village is still called the gate of blood. The dictionary puts both in one entry because they are opposite errors and opposite fates: a theory of a new age that superseded the written word, and a village that died for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an age as a period of time; prophecy as a foretelling; the millennium as the thousand years of Revelation; a village as a small assemblage of houses; and a massacre as the murder of many.
webster_full: AGE, n. The whole duration of a being; a certain period of human life; a century; a particular period of time.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come; in Scripture, an instruction or exhortation under divine inspiration.
MILLENNIUM, n. A thousand years; a word used to denote the thousand years mentioned in Revelation xx, during which holiness is to be triumphant.
VILLAGE, n. A small assemblage of houses, less than a town or city, and inhabited chiefly by farmers and other laboring people.
MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with cruelty or atrocity.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Heb 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
corruption_summary: Region of the Italian toe, home of Joachim of Fiore's three ages and of the Waldensian village of Guardia Piemontese destroyed in 1561.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the doctrine of a new age that outranks the text, which is Joachim's legacy and is everywhere in modern religion under other names. Once history is divided into ages with a rising spiritual content, the writings of the apostles become the charter of a superseded period, and whatever the present age is said to require can be asserted without them. Scripture closes that door twice: the deposit was handed over once, so believers must “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and additions are forbidden in the same breath as subtractions, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the unchangeableness of Christ and therefore of the gospel about him: “Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever” (Heb 13:8). A people who held that in a Calabrian village while a viceroy's troops came up the hill had better theology than the abbot of Fiore, and the dictionary says so without apology. John's altar is where they are: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9). The village gate still carries the name the killing gave it, which is a sort of testimony the inhabitants never chose and could not have refused.

pos: n. (the island kingdom where Paul was shipwrecked nearby and landed at Syracuse, and where the Spanish Inquisition was established in 1487)
etymology: From Latin Sicilia, from the Siculi, the people of the island.
biblical_def: Sicily is the largest island of the Mediterranean and the oldest crossroads in it: Greek, Carthaginian, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Norman, Angevin, Aragonese and Spanish in turn. It has a biblical mention, since Paul's ship from Malta put in at Syracuse for three days on the voyage to Rome. Under the Normans it held Greek, Latin and Arabic populations in a single kingdom, and under Frederick the Second a court of extraordinary learning. From 1282 it belonged to Aragon and so to Spain, and in 1487 the Spanish Inquisition was established on the island with its own tribunal at Palermo, outside the authority of the Roman Holy Office, which gave Sicily one of the most thorough religious police systems in Europe. The result is that no evangelical movement of any size ever formed there. The dictionary records Sicily as the counter-example to Tuscany and Venice: an Italian territory where the machinery was in place a generation before Luther, and where the gospel therefore had no reading public to reach. The island is not evidence that the word fails. It is evidence of what a tribunal can do when it starts early.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an island as a tract of land surrounded by water; an inquisition as a court for the examination of heretics; a tribunal as the seat of a judge; conquest as the act of subduing; and shipwreck as the destruction of a vessel.
webster_full: ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; a smaller portion of land surrounded by water than a continent.
INQUISITION, n. In some catholic countries, a court or tribunal established for the examination and punishment of heretics.
TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.
CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by war or force.
SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship by being cast ashore or broken to pieces by beating against rocks.
scriptures: And landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days.
Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: Mediterranean island where Paul landed at Syracuse, and where the Spanish Inquisition was established in 1487, a generation before Luther.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the argument from absence: because no Reformation took root in Sicily, the island is used to prove that Italians were simply uninterested, or that the Roman religion suited the Mediterranean temperament. The dictionary answers with a date. The Spanish Inquisition was functioning at Palermo in 1487, with familiars in every town and a tribunal independent of Rome, thirty years before the theses. There was no reading public left to reach, which is a political fact and not a spiritual verdict. The word itself is not confined by such arrangements: “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that God's word is tied to his sending and not to our conditions, “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). The dictionary also notes with pleasure that the island's first recorded Christian visit was an apostle in custody on his way to trial, whose ship “landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days” (Act 28:12), and that Luke ends the book with the same man under guard and the preaching unhindered: “Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him” (Act 28:31). Sicily began with a prisoner who could not be silenced.

pos: n. (the island kingdom held by Aragon and Spain with its own Inquisition tribunal, and from 1720 the nucleus of the Savoyard kingdom)
etymology: From Latin Sardinia, from the Sardi, the people of the island.
biblical_def: Sardinia is the second island of the Mediterranean, mountainous, pastoral and long isolated, with its own Romance language. It was Byzantine, then governed by four native judicates, then conquered by Aragon in the fourteenth century and held by Spain until 1708. A tribunal of the Spanish Inquisition sat at Sassari and Cagliari. In 1720 the island was exchanged to the house of Savoy, whose dukes took from it the title king of Sardinia; the Savoyard state that persecuted the Waldensian valleys and later unified Italy therefore carried this island's name. The island's Christianity is ancient, with martyrs under Diocletian and a monastic tradition, and it was also a place of deportation: Callistus and other Roman Christians were sent to its mines under Commodus, and Hippolytus and Pontian both died there as exiles in 235. The dictionary records Sardinia as a mine and a prison as much as a kingdom. Some of the church's earliest confessors ended in its quarries, which is a useful corrective to any account of early Christianity that forgets how much of it happened to slaves.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mine as a pit from which minerals are taken; deportation as transportation or exile; a confessor as one who avows his religion under persecution; bondage as slavery; and patience as the suffering of afflictions without murmuring.
webster_full: MINE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, from which metallic ores, mineral substances and other fossil bodies are taken.
DEPORTATION, n. Transportation; a removal from one country to another, or to a distant place; exile; banishment.
CONFESSOR, n. One who makes a profession of his faith in the christian religion; one who avows his religion in the face of danger.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty by compulsion.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: Mediterranean island held by Aragon and Spain with its own Inquisition tribunal, a Roman penal colony to whose mines early confessors including Pontian and Hippolytus were deported.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour due to the obscure confessor. Sardinia's mines took Christians who were not bishops of great sees and left no writings, and alongside them took two Roman churchmen who had been at odds with each other and died in the same exile. Hebrews gives the whole company a single commendation that makes no distinction of rank: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to read church history as a succession of names and to lose the mass of the faithful. Scripture will not allow it. The victory it describes belongs to a company, not to individuals, “And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11), and the writer to the Hebrews pictures the present church running inside a crowd of such witnesses, “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1). Peter addresses ordinary scattered believers with the titles of a priesthood, “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9), which is what the men in the quarries were.

pos: n. (the island held by Genoa and from 1769 by France, whose brief independent constitution of 1755 was the first to invoke the people under God)
etymology: From Latin Corsica, from the Corsi, the people of the island.
biblical_def: Corsica is a mountainous island north of Sardinia, held by Pisa and then from 1284 by Genoa, in near-continuous revolt from 1729, briefly independent under Pasquale Paoli from 1755, and conquered by France in 1769. Paoli's constitution of 1755 is the island's claim on this dictionary: a written frame of government with a representative assembly, drafted a generation before the American and French constitutions, which opened by placing the nation under God and was admired by Rousseau and by Boswell, who visited Paoli and made him famous in Britain. Paoli himself was a serious man of Christian conviction and an unusual ruler in that he gave up power rather than hold it by blood. The island had no Reformation; it was Genoese, Catholic, and remote from the presses. The dictionary records Corsica for the constitution, and because Paoli illustrates a point the Reformed tradition has always pressed: that written limits on power are a mercy to a people, and that the men who establish them are usually men who believe they will answer to someone higher.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a constitution as the established form of government; a covenant as a mutual agreement; liberty as freedom from restraint; an assembly as a company met together; and accountability as liableness to answer.
webster_full: CONSTITUTION, n. The established form of government in a state, kingdom or country; the system of fundamental rules and principles by which a nation is governed.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; civil liberty is the not being restrained by any law but what conduces in a greater degree to the public welfare.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, and usually for some common purpose.
ACCOUNTABLENESS, n. The state of being liable to answer for one's conduct; liability to give account.
scriptures: Dan 2:21
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
corruption_summary: Mediterranean island held by Genoa and then France, whose 1755 constitution under Pasquale Paoli placed a representative government under God a generation before the great revolutions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that constitutions are written by men who expect to be judged. Paoli's frame of 1755 began by invoking God and was obeyed by its author when it limited him, which is rarer than the document. Scripture states the fact that makes any such limit intelligible: “And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21). A ruler who believes that will accept an assembly; a ruler who does not will keep an army.

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to trust a document or a leader instead of the one who gives both. The psalmist forbids it in the plainest words, “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3), and Solomon ties a nation's standing not to its constitution but to its character: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). What is asked of the man who governs is the same thing asked of the man who does not, reduced to three clauses, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). Corsica lost its independence in fourteen years; the dictionary keeps the document anyway.

pos: n. (the Sicilian capital, seat of the Norman kings and of the Spanish Inquisition tribunal whose prison walls still carry the prisoners' writings)
etymology: From Greek Panormos, the all-harbour, from pan and hormos, an anchorage.
biblical_def: Palermo is the capital of Sicily, a Phoenician foundation, an Arab emirate's capital in the tenth century, and from 1072 the seat of the Norman kings whose court mixed Latin, Greek and Arabic clerks and whose chapel mosaics are among the finest in Christendom. From 1487 it was the seat of the Sicilian tribunal of the Spanish Inquisition, housed after 1601 in the Palazzo Steri, whose cells preserve inscriptions, drawings, prayers and verses scratched and written on the plaster by prisoners over a century and a half, including many by men held for religious offences. The tribunal was abolished in 1782. The dictionary records Palermo because those walls are a primary source of a very rare kind: the words of the examined rather than the examiners. The register of a trial tells you the charge; the plaster tells you what the charged man wrote when he was alone. Several of the inscriptions are prayers, several are protests of innocence, and several are simply dates counted out, which is what a man does when nobody is coming.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prison as a house for the confinement of offenders; an inscription as something written or engraved; examination as a judicial inquiry; innocence as freedom from guilt; and hope as a desire of good with expectation of obtaining it.
webster_full: PRISON, n. A house or place of confinement, particularly for debtors and criminals; a jail; a place of involuntary restraint.
INSCRIPTION, n. Something written or engraved, to communicate knowledge to after ages; a title; a motto.
EXAMINATION, n. A careful search or inquiry; a judicial inquiry; the act of interrogating a person on oath.
INNOCENCE, n. Freedom from guilt or legal offense; untainted purity of heart and life.
HOPE, n. A desire of some good, accompanied with at least a slight expectation of obtaining it, or a belief that it is obtainable.
scriptures: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
Dan 6:10

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
corruption_summary: Sicilian capital and seat of the Spanish Inquisition tribunal from 1487, whose Palazzo Steri cells preserve the inscriptions prisoners wrote on the plaster.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the religious prison, and the dictionary names it as a contradiction rather than an excess. A tribunal that holds a man in a cell until he says what it requires has not established the truth of anything, since a confession extracted in those conditions carries no information at all. What it does establish is on the walls. The psalm of the captives is written by men in exactly that position, remembering a place they cannot see: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion” (Psa 137:1).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the duty of the free church toward the imprisoned one. Hebrews makes it a matter of imagination and not merely of charity, charging believers to “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3). The posture Daniel takes when the writing is signed against him is the posture the Steri plaster records in scratched prayers: “he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10). And what Peter requires of a man under question is an answer, given with a particular manner, “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15) — which is the opposite of what a torture chamber is designed to produce.

pos: n. (the Sicilian port at the strait where the Jesuits opened their first college in 1548, the model for the order's whole educational system)
etymology: From Greek Messene, renamed from Zankle, the sickle, for the shape of its harbour.
biblical_def: Messina stands at the strait between Sicily and the mainland and has always lived by it. Its place in this dictionary is educational. In 1548 the city magistrates asked Ignatius Loyola for teachers, and the Jesuits opened at Messina the first college in the history of the order designed to educate lay boys as well as its own novices — free of charge, with a graded curriculum, regular examinations, public disputations and a strict progression of classes. The Ratio studiorum of 1599 systematised what was worked out at Messina, and within a century the order ran several hundred colleges across Europe and the mission fields. The dictionary records this with respect and without softening its judgment. The Jesuit school was the most effective instrument the Roman church ever built, and it was built to recover from the Reformation what argument had not recovered: a generation of boys. Protestants who sneer at it have usually not matched it. The Reformed answer was the parish school and the catechism, and where those were kept the ground held.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of scholars; a curriculum is not in Webster, but a course is a series of proceedings; a disputation as a controversy in words; a novice as one newly admitted; and education as the bringing up of a child.
webster_full: COLLEGE, n. A society of persons engaged in the pursuits of literature, including the officers and students; the edifice occupied by such a society.
COURSE, n. A series of proceedings; the order of succession; a methodical series, as a course of lectures.
DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words; controversy in words; an exercise in colleges in which parties reason in opposition to each other.
NOVICE, n. One who is new in any business; one newly admitted to membership in a religious house; a probationer.

EDUCATION, n. The bringing up, as of a child; instruction; formation of manners; comprehending all that series of instruction and discipline which is intended to enlighten the understanding and correct the temper.
scriptures: Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
corruption_summary: Sicilian port where the Jesuits opened their first lay college in 1548, the model for the order's educational system and its most effective instrument.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the outsourcing of a child's formation, and it is a Protestant failing at least as much as a Roman one. The Messina model worked because it took the teaching of boys seriously, every day, in a fixed order, for years. Where Protestants left that to chance they lost the next generation and then blamed the schoolmaster. Scripture puts the duty in the household first and makes it constant rather than scheduled: “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The thing to be taught is the text, and Paul describes Timothy's advantage as an early acquaintance with it, “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15). The charge falls on fathers by name, who are to bring their children up “in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and Solomon attaches a promise to early formation that no institution can supply on a parent's behalf: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). The dictionary concludes that the right reply to Messina was never to close a school but to keep a catechism.

pos: n. (the Sicilian city under Etna, rebuilt after the eruption of 1669 and the earthquake of 1693, and seat of the island's oldest university)
etymology: From Greek Katane, a Chalcidian colony of 729 before Christ, the name of Sicel origin.
biblical_def: Catania lies on the east coast of Sicily beneath Etna and has been destroyed repeatedly: by the lava flow of 1669 which reached the sea through the city, and by the earthquake of 1693 which killed a large part of the population of eastern Sicily. It was rebuilt each time on the same ground, in the baroque that now gives the city its character, and its university, founded in 1434, is the oldest on the island. The dictionary records Catania for the sake of the question a city under a volcano forces. Scripture does not permit the reading of particular disasters as particular verdicts on particular people, and Christ says so explicitly about a tower that fell and a massacre in the temple. It also does not permit the modern move of treating such events as meaningless. They are summons. Catania's people rebuilt under the mountain, which is what men do and is not wrong; the dictionary only insists that a city which has twice been buried has been spoken to, and that the content of the speech is repentance rather than information about the dead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a volcano as a burning mountain; an earthquake as a shaking of the earth; calamity as any great misfortune; providence as the care of God over his creatures; and repentance as sorrow for sin with amendment.
webster_full: VOLCANO, n. A burning mountain; a mountain that vomits or has vomited fire, smoke, cinders, ashes and lava.
EARTHQUAKE, n. A shaking, trembling or concussion of the earth; sometimes a slight tremor, at other times a violent shaking.
CALAMITY, n. Any great misfortune or cause of misery; generally applied to events or disasters which produce extensive evils.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a providing or preparing beforehand.
REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, with a sincere purpose of amendment.
scriptures: Luk 13:4
Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?
Luk 13:5
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
Amo 4:12
Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
Psa 46:2
Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea;
corruption_summary: Sicilian city beneath Etna, destroyed by the lava of 1669 and the earthquake of 1693 and rebuilt on the same ground, seat of the island's oldest university.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name has two forms and the dictionary rejects both. The first reads a disaster as a judgment on its victims, which Christ forbids by name, asking of eighteen men killed by a falling tower whether they were sinners “above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?” (Luk 13:4). The second treats the event as pure mechanism with no address in it, which is the modern instinct and is equally unavailable, because Christ's own conclusion from the tower is a command to everybody else: “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luk 13:5).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a city under a mountain is in the same position as every other city, only more visibly. Amos states the summons in the form it always takes, “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel” (Amo 4:12), and the psalmist supplies the courage to live there, refusing fear in the exact scenario Catania keeps living through: “Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea” (Psa 46:2). The dictionary honours the Catanesi for rebuilding; it declines to pretend the mountain said nothing.

pos: n. (the Campanian see whose bishop Victor of Capua recovered and published the gospel harmony now known as the Fulda codex)
etymology: From Latin Capua, an Etruscan and Oscan city of Campania, of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Capua was the chief city of Campania in antiquity, celebrated for its wealth, infamous for the gladiatorial school from which Spartacus broke out, destroyed by the Saracens in 841 and rebuilt a few miles away. Its contribution to the Scriptures of the church is a book. Victor, bishop of Capua in the mid sixth century, found an old Latin gospel harmony, recognised it as a translation of the work of Tatian, and had it copied with his own preface; that copy travelled north, was owned by Boniface, and survives at Fulda as the chief Latin witness to the Diatessaron, the second-century weaving of the four gospels into one continuous narrative. The dictionary records Capua for Victor's instinct, which was a scholar's and a bishop's at once: he did not destroy an irregular book, and he did not canonise it either. He identified it, dated it, prefaced it and preserved it. A harmony is a useful study tool and is not Scripture, because the four gospels are four and the church has never been given leave to replace them with one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a harmony as the just adaptation of parts, and in Scripture the agreement of the evangelists; a codex is not in Webster, but a manuscript is a written book; a preface as an introduction; a witness as testimony; and a canon as a rule of the church.
webster_full: HARMONY, n. The just adaptation of parts to each other; in theology, a work in which the four gospels are brought into one continuous narrative.
MANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing not printed.
PREFACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book, containing the design of the author.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
CANON, n. In an ecclesiastical sense, the authorized catalogue of the sacred writings; a law or rule of doctrine.
scriptures: Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
corruption_summary: Campanian see whose bishop Victor identified, prefaced and preserved the Latin gospel harmony now surviving as the Fulda codex of the Diatessaron.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right handling of a useful book that is not Scripture. Victor of Capua neither burned the harmony nor read it in church; he catalogued it. Harmonies, concordances, commentaries and catechisms all stand in that class, serviceable and not inspired, and the line matters because the text itself fences its own boundary: “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to prefer a smooth single narrative to four accounts that do not always run in the same order. The dictionary holds that the fourfold shape is itself given. Luke states his own method as orderly inquiry into what others had already written, “It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3), and John names his purpose in writing a gospel that leaves much out, “that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (Joh 20:31). What is inspired is the writing, not our arrangement of it: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16).

pos: n. (the Campanian port whose medical school was the first in medieval Europe, and the place where Gregory the Seventh died in exile in 1085)
etymology: From Latin Salernum, a Roman colony of 194 before Christ, of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Salerno is a port south of Naples which held the first and for two centuries the foremost medical school of Latin Europe, drawing on Greek and Arabic texts translated at nearby Monte Cassino and producing the Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a verse manual of health that was copied and printed for five hundred years. Its school admitted women as practitioners, which almost nowhere else did. Salerno is also where Gregory the Seventh died on the twenty-fifth of May 1085, driven from Rome by the emperor Henry the Fourth and sheltered by the Norman duke Robert Guiscard; his reported last words were that he had loved righteousness and hated iniquity and therefore died in exile. The dictionary records both. Gregory's reform was genuine in its attack on simony and clerical marriage-money and ruinous in its claim that the pope may depose kings, and the two cannot be separated in him. A man may spend his life fighting a real corruption with a weapon that becomes the next corruption, and Salerno is where that man died.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines medicine as the art of healing; a regimen as the regulation of diet; investiture as the act of giving possession; exile as banishment; and righteousness as purity of heart and rectitude of life.
webster_full: MEDICINE, n. Any substance administered to a sick person with a view to cure; the art of preventing, curing or alleviating diseases.
REGIMEN, n. In medicine, the regulation of diet with a view to the preservation or restoration of health.
INVESTITURE, n. The act of giving possession of lands or of an office, or of a benefice, with its appropriate ceremonies.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
scriptures: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Campanian port of medieval Europe's first medical school, and the place of Gregory the Seventh's death in exile in 1085.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the papal claim to depose princes, which Gregory the Seventh asserted and which set the pattern for five centuries of conflict. The dictionary grants that his target was real: bishoprics were bought, benefices sold, offices inherited, and somebody had to attack it. What he reached for was a jurisdiction over crowns, and Christ had already excluded that pattern of authority for his servants in so many words: “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that spiritual authority has its own instruments and loses itself when it borrows the state's. Christ grounds the refusal in the nature of his kingdom, “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36), and Paul describes the church's armoury as effective precisely because it is not political: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). Gregory died saying he had loved righteousness; the dictionary takes him at his word and sets beside it the prophet's summary of what righteousness actually required of him, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8).

“My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — the ground of the refusal.
“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — what righteousness actually required.
